 Shipping GST Relief Targets Overseas Group Services as CBIC Clarifies Tax Rules
 October 30, 2026 
 6:19 am 
 Maritime Gateway 
 ChatGPT 
 Perplexity 
 Claude 
 Grok 
 Twitter 
 Facebook 
 LinkedIn 
 WhatsApp 
 Email 
 Summary
 CBIC has clarified GST treatment across shipping, vehicle leasing, research and banking services. For Indian establishments of foreign shipping companies, specified overseas services received without consideration will be exempt from 1 November 2026, while the circular regularises past GST treatment. Other clarifications address leasing recoveries, research grants and financial services.
 Exemption covers specified overseas shipping-company services
 Shipping GST relief will apply from 1 November 2026 to services imported without consideration by Indian establishments of foreign shipping companies from related persons or their other establishments outside India.
 The exemption is introduced through Notification No. 07/2026-Integrated Tax (Rate), dated 27 October. It inserts a specific entry into the existing integrated-tax exemption framework.
 Its scope is defined by the recipient, the overseas supplier’s relationship with that recipient and the absence of consideration. It does not provide a general exemption for freight, shipping agency services or every transaction involving a foreign shipping company.
 Earlier period receives separate treatment
 Circular No. 266/12/2026-GST, dated 28 October, regularises GST payments for the specified shipping-company transactions between 1 July 2017 and 31 October 2026 on an “as is where is” basis.
 The circular follows recommendations adopted at the GST Council’s 57th meeting on 8 October. It also addresses vehicle leasing, research and development, banking, co-lending and the status of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India.
 The prospective exemption and past-period regularisation are separate measures, with 1 November marking the transition between them.
 Why services without payment can raise GST questions
 The underlying issue arises from the treatment of certain transactions between related entities.
 Schedule I of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act includes imports of services from a related person or another overseas establishment, in the course or furtherance of business, among activities treated as supplies even without consideration.
 Consequently, the absence of an invoice payment does not, by itself, remove such a transaction from GST.
 The new shipping exemption addresses a defined category within that framework. Its practical significance lies in giving qualifying establishments a specific exemption rather than leaving their position to be determined solely under the general rules for transactions without consideration.
 Leasing recoveries form part of the taxable service
 For motor vehicle leasing, CBIC has clarified that separately recovered registration charges, road tax, insurance premiums, FASTag charges and similar incidental expenses form part of the composite leasing supply.
 They attract the rate applicable to the motor vehicle leasing service.
 The circular also distinguishes research from consultancy: a certificate from the head of an eligible institution confirming that grant-funded work constitutes research and development may suffice for the relevant exemption.
 In banking, qualifying notional interest under the Fund Transfer Pricing mechanism falls within the interest exemption. By contrast, services supplied by NBFCs to banks under co-lending arrangements are taxable, valued according to their contractual agreement.
 TRAI, meanwhile, does not qualify as “Government” under the specified CGST Act definition.
 Wider reforms provide the policy background
 The October GST Council meeting placed these sector-specific decisions within a broader programme of procedural reform.
 Its recommendations covered registration, return reconciliation, refunds, adjudication and trade facilitation. For businesses moving goods across states, the agenda included more consistent enforcement procedures and smoother cargo movement.
 The Council also recommended an exemption for services supplied by the Seamen’s Provident Fund Organisation to persons governed by the Seamen’s Provident Fund Act, 1966.
 Importantly, the Council’s announcement distinguished recommendations from enforceable changes: implementation depends on the relevant notifications, circulars or legislative amendments.
 That distinction matters for logistics businesses reviewing several announcements together. Each measure has its own scope, conditions and implementation instrument; a Council recommendation alone does not establish an effective date.
 Implications for shipping and logistics businesses
 For qualifying shipping establishments, the central task is identifying which overseas arrangements meet the exemption’s conditions. Related-party services supplied for consideration require separate examination.
 Vehicle lessors and their customers also need to account for incidental recoveries when assessing the taxable value of leasing arrangements.
 Taken together, the measures address different questions: whether a supply is exempt, which charges belong in its value and how earlier periods are treated. Their commercial effect will depend on the transaction structure and the applicable provision, rather than a single sector-wide change in GST rates.
 FAQs
 When does the shipping exemption begin?
 It takes effect on 1 November 2026.
 Which shipping transactions qualify?
 Specified services received without consideration by Indian establishments of foreign shipping companies from related persons or their other overseas establishments.
 Does the measure exempt all shipping services?
 No. It covers a defined category of imported services.
 What period does the regularisation cover?
 From 1 July 2017 to 31 October 2026.
 How are incidental vehicle-leasing recoveries treated?
 They form part of the composite leasing supply and attract the applicable leasing rate.
